issues.item: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, a trigger based on being in a similar natural environment is hard to reconcile unless the robbery specifically occurred in wilderness or outdoors; nothing else in the profile supports that context, making this trigger clinically incongruent with the rest of the presentation.

Helicopter/aircraft sounds are not a plausible trauma-linked trigger for a mugging/robbery in the absence of any supporting memory or threat content suggesting emergency-response, combat, or disaster context. This appears disconnected from the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to link clinically unless the robbery specifically involved aircraft or a major police response; this trigger is not supported by the other selected items and feels trauma-incongruent.

Alcohol smell could occur if the perpetrator had been drinking, but that link is not reflected anywhere else in the profile, so as selected it appears weakly grounded in the trauma narrative compared with the other more plausible interpersonal-danger cues.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma in a 67-year-old male, contamination and body-focused shame are hard to reconcile unless there was a sexual assault or severe bodily violation component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. These appraisals fit poorly with the stated trauma type and with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Burnt smell is a highly specific trigger that suggests fire, smoke, or explosion exposure. In a robbery/mugging profile it lacks support from the threat and appraisal items and does not connect plausibly to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery in a 67-year-old male, 'body shame' is hard to reconcile unless there was prominent sexual assault, disfigurement, or injury-focused trauma content, which is not reflected elsewhere in threat, memory, or strategies. It reads as a qualitatively different appraisal from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: 'Burnt smell' is not a plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery unless there was specific fire/smoke/burning content in the trauma, which is not supported by the other selected items. It appears disconnected from the stated trauma type and from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery victim, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the report centers on external danger and mistrust (suspicious people, loud noises, hypervigilance, alarm when touched, mistrust, humiliation), but this item implies morally dissonant behaviour by the patient during the event. That is possible, but without any supporting memory or strategy content it stands apart from the otherwise victimization-focused formulation and is harder to reconcile clinically than the other items. The remaining items are broadly coherent with robbery trauma and with the active formulation path Negative Appraisals → Threat and Threat → Triggers.

vignette: Thomas had been a hotel manager for thirty years, a man who prided himself on knowing every corridor, every guest, every staff member's name. The night he was mugged, the hallway he walked each evening with the key card to the executive lounge was suddenly an alley of strangers. A young man in a hoodie appeared from the shadows, demanded Thomas's wallet, and when Thomas refused to give it up, the attacker lunged with a knife. The confrontation ended with Thomas's wallet in the man's hand and a bruised thumb, but the damage was not just physical. Thomas felt the sting of humiliation the instant he realized he had been taken in his own establishment, the feeling that his professional identity had been publicly stripped away. In the days that followed he began to think that people could not be trusted; that the world, once a place of hospitality and routine, was now a dangerous arena. Those negative appraisals-mistrust, humiliation, a world in which danger lurked-were the seeds that sprouted his constant state of alertness. From that point onward, Thomas's perception of threat dominated his thoughts. The belief that every stranger might want his wallet or his valuables meant that he was always super-alert, constantly scanning. He became hypervigilant; a single sound could set his heart racing, and he reacted with alarm when a colleague touched his arm for the first time in months. Even in the quiet of his own home, he felt a persistent need to check that every door was locked, every window was secure, and he lay awake in the dark, listening to the faint creak of the floorboards as if a thief could be listening too. When he returned to the hotel each morning, those heightened threat perceptions turned the ordinary into potential danger. A guest walking past the reception desk would trigger a flinch; a man in a business suit walking past the elevators would make Thomas's eyes flicker to the door as if expecting a threat. The smell of alcohol coming from the staff lounge or the bar during a busy evening became a cue that danger might be imminent. Loud noises-whether a sudden burst of laughter in the dining room or the clatter of plates-would set his hands trembling, and he would pause in the doorway, heart hammering, before he could speak to a guest. The triggers he was now sensitive to were not random; they were the manifestations of the threat state that his negative appraisals had cemented. Whenever a suspicious face appeared or the scent of alcohol drifted through the hallway, Thomas's hypervigilance made him see danger where it had not been before, and his body responded with a startle to touch that kept him perpetually on edge. The cycle tightened further as Thomas began to avoid the very situations that might help him feel safe. He began to refuse to stay late when the bar was busy, to keep his staff's access to the guest rooms restricted, and to ask his wife to stay out of the hotel after hours. He stopped participating in staff meetings that were held in the lounge, fearing the alcohol smell and the loud conversations. In the evenings, he would not go to the local pub with friends because he imagined the people might act suspiciously or that a stranger might approach him on the sidewalk. Each avoidance solidified his perception of the world as unsafe and increased his sense of humiliation for being unable to engage normally. The hypervigilant, startle-prone Thomas found himself unable to relax even when he was at home, constantly on guard, feeling the weight of his past event on every creak and every scent. Now, at the age of sixty-seven, Thomas sits in a therapist's office, eyes darting as he speaks of the mugging. He tells the therapist that he feels "sick" whenever someone near him appears uneasy, and that the smell of beer makes him feel as if someone is plotting to take his life. He admits that he has begun to withdraw from his wife's visits to the hotel, afraid that she might witness his erratic behavior or that someone else might see him as a target. His marriage, once a source of comfort, has become a source of anxiety because he cannot trust his partner's presence to calm him. The fear that he will once again be humiliated or robbed has kept him from sleeping peacefully, and his exhaustion has made him less efficient at managing his staff. When he looks at the ledger of his hotel, he sees not only numbers but a ledger of threats that he must constantly monitor. Thomas's most urgent hope is to feel safe again-both in the corridors of the hotel he manages and in his own home. His greatest fear is that one day the triggers he has become attuned to will strike again, that another assault will bring his world back to that night in the hallway, and that his reputation as a competent, trustworthy manager will crumble. It is this desperate longing for safety and stability that finally led him to seek help, hoping that the weight of the negative appraisals will loosen and that the constant threat will no longer dictate every moment of his life.
